summary: Recommends using 127-bit IPv6 prefixes on point-to-point links between routers, similar to 31-bit prefixes in IPv4, and explains the motivation. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6164 allows IPv6 routers to use a /127 prefix on a point-to-point link between two routers. The smaller prefix avoids risks created by many unused addresses, provided routers disable Subnet-Router anycast on that prefix.

subtitle: Why router-to-router point-to-point IPv6 links can use a /127 prefix, and what routers must do.

tldr.problem: Long IPv6 prefixes on router links had been discouraged, but a /64 can expose routers to forwarding loops and neighbor-cache exhaustion.
tldr.mechanism: Routers must support /127 prefixes on point-to-point inter-router links and disable Subnet-Router anycast for that prefix; operators must also avoid reserved anycast addresses when sharing a /64.
tldr.outcome: The RFC supports /127 use on inter-router links and updates the earlier guidance. It was updated by RFC 6547.

today: RFC 6164 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011. It has been updated by RFC 6547.

sections.title: Why Use a /127 Prefix
sections.content:
Earlier IPv6 guidance discouraged 127-bit prefixes because they could conflict with the Subnet-Router anycast address. RFC 6164 reconsiders that concern and describes how to use /127 prefixes on inter-router point-to-point links. The approach parallels 31-bit prefixes on IPv4 point-to-point links.

This guidance applies when operators assign specific addresses on links between exactly two routers. Such addresses may support monitoring, reverse DNS or routing sessions. Links to hosts and links using only link-local addresses are outside the recommendation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers on a point-to-point link can use a /127 prefix instead of a much larger address block. This recommendation does not cover links that also connect hosts.

sections.title: Earlier Concerns About /127
sections.content: RFC 3627 discouraged /127 prefixes because of Subnet-Router anycast. RFC 5375 also said they were invalid and strongly discouraged, citing the earlier document. RFC 6164 accepts that those analyses were correct but says operational experience showed that /127 prefixes could be used successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier documents warned against /127 prefixes because of an anycast conflict. This RFC says that routers can use them successfully when they follow its rules.

sections.title: Forwarding Loops and Cache Exhaustion
sections.content:
On some point-to-point links without Neighbor Discovery, a prefix shorter than /127 can allow a packet to loop back and forth. A forwarding rule in the cited ICMPv6 specification requires a router not to send such a packet back over the link it arrived on; the check may affect forwarding performance.

On an Ethernet link using a /64, packets sent to unused addresses can make a router create incomplete neighbor-cache entries and send Neighbor Solicitation messages. A stream aimed at many unused addresses can consume memory and processing. Assigning a /127 subnet eliminates this neighbor-cache exhaustion issue described here.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger prefix can leave many unused addresses that trigger neighbor checks. A /127 sharply limits those addresses and avoids that cache-exhaustion attack on the link.

sections.title: Router and Addressing Requirements
sections.content:
Routers must support assigning /127 prefixes on point-to-point inter-router links. When they use /127, they must disable Subnet-Router anycast for that prefix.

When operators number multiple links out of one /64, addresses with all zeros in the rightmost 64 bits should not be assigned as unicast. The highest 128 values in those 64 bits should also not be used as unicast, because they are reserved subnet anycast addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers must support /127 prefixes and turn off Subnet-Router anycast on them. If several links share a /64, operators should keep the reserved anycast addresses out of unicast use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no security considerations of its own. It discusses two security-related problems with longer prefixes on inter-router links: forwarding loops and neighbor-cache exhaustion. Its /127 recommendation addresses those problems in the described settings.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's security discussion concerns the loop and cache-exhaustion risks described earlier. It recommends /127 prefixes as a way to address them on covered links.
